summary: The article surveys tools and techniques for forecasting space weather to predict and mitigate service outages affecting power grids, GPS and communications. It covers better solar observation equipment, more sophisticated models, machine learning, international collaboration, grid hardening, GPS backup standards and public awareness, with quotes from several experts. It concludes that outages from solar activity may become manageable or preventable.
one_line: Overview of advances in space weather forecasting, from observatories and machine learning to collaboration and grid hardening, aimed at reducing solar-driven service outages.
key_facts: Space weather refers to environmental conditions in space influenced by the Sun and solar wind that can affect satellites, GPS, power grids and radio communications.
Solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and high-speed solar wind streams can create geomagnetic storms when interacting with Earth's magnetosphere.
In September 2023 a significant CME caused widespread GPS malfunctions in North America, prompting NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) to intensify forecasting efforts.
Dr. Linda Rothschild said on October 5th, 2023 that the incident was a 'wake-up call for improving our prediction tools.'
The Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) and Parker Solar Probe provide high-resolution images and in-situ measurements of solar activity.
NOAA's Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCOVR), launched in June 2023, delivers real-time solar wind data.
Dr. Emily Tran said on November 22nd, 2023 that improved simulations allow warnings tailored to the type of satellite, grid or communication system at risk.
Dr. Jason Clark said on December 1st, 2023 that machine learning uncovers subtle precursors to major disruptions and turns predictions into actionable alerts.
The European Space Agency (ESA) has joined forces with NOAA to share data and resources; ESA's Dr. Anita Schmidt said on December 15th, 2023 that 'No single entity can tackle space weather alone.'
On January 4th, 2024, Dr. Robert Hanson said the goal is to design power systems that are inherently resilient to geomagnetic disruptions.
On January 20th, 2024, the FAA and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) took part in a symposium on new standards and backup systems for GPS-dependent navigation.
On February 5th, 2024, Dr. Karen Zhou said informing the public about space weather is as important as forecasting weather on Earth.
